senses.gloss:
kūṭaślokas
(‘verses with enigmatic meaning’)
------------------------------------------
The Mahābhārata, the great epic of the Hindus, has a large number of verses whose meaning is quite enigmatic. Their actual etymological meaning and the sense they try to convey are not only different but may even appear opposed to each other. Such verses or ślokas are called ‘kūṭaślokas’.
According to the Ādiparva (1.79-83) the sage व्यास requested गणपति, the god of learning, to take down the text of the Mahābhārata as he went on reciting. गणपति laid down the condition that व्यास should never stop reciting so that he could write it continuously. व्यास put a counter-condition that गणपति should understand the full meaning of the śloka first, before writing it down. Whenever व्यास needed some time to think of the next śloka, he would compose a ‘kūṭaśloka,’ a śloka with a difficult or double meaning—and hence enigmatic—to keep गणपति guessing and thinking about it before writing it down with his stylus. During the interval he managed to get thus, he would compose the next śloka of the text!.
According to the Mahābhārata itself (Ādiparva 1.81) there are 8,800 कूटश्लोकस् in the work.
One example can make this more clear:
Duryodhana the wily genius, has planned to destroy his cousins, the Pāṇḍavas—whom he considers as his arch-enemies—by setting fire to a palace at the city of Vāraṇāvata which he has got built with highly combustible substances like lac and straw. He has cleverly managed to make them agree to the proposal of retiring to that city and live in that palace, the proposal itself coming from धृतराष्ट्र. The Pāṇḍavas readily agree. Just before their departure, विदुर, the wise minister of the Kauravas and a great well-wisher of the Pāṇḍavas warns युधिष्ठिर (the eldest and the shrewdest of the Pāṇḍavas) of the impending danger and also suggests the solutions (vide Ādiparva, 145.20 to 26). Out of these, only one verse (145.22) may be cited.
Direct translation: ‘One who knows about that weapon of the enemy which is sharp and capable of killing, though not made out of metal, will not be killed (or harmed) by it’.
The hidden meaning, however, is:
‘One who knows that the होउसे (or the palace) though made up of combustible materials, has camouflaged itself (nicely) and will destroy him in the night, will not be killed by the enemies.’
Yudhiṣṭhira gets the hint, takes remedial measures and successfully escapes the arson attempt, along with his मोथेर् and brothers.
See also VANAPARVA 188.42.
